Apps / Taskbar / AppX
SafeInventory
Get-AppxPackage Microsoft.Windows.StartMenuExperienceHost
Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | select DisplayName,PackageName

AppX/provisioned-package cmdlets diagnose Start menu, taskbar, and built-in-app problems tied to a corrupted or missing package.

Get-AppxPackage — Microsoft Learn ↗ Add-AppxPackage — Microsoft Learn ↗ MSIX/AppX deployment overview — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Minor changeRepair / remove
Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | ? DisplayName -like "*AppName*" | Remove-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online

Get-AppxPackage Microsoft.Windows.Photos | % {
  Add-AppxPackage -DisableDevelopmentMode -Register "$($_.InstallLocation)\AppXManifest.xml"
}

Removing a provisioned package doesn't remove an existing user install.

Re-registering re-links an installed app's manifest to the current user profile — the standard fix for a broken built-in Windows app.

Big changeRe-register all current-user AppX
Get-AppxPackage | % {
  Add-AppxPackage -DisableDevelopmentMode -Register "$($_.InstallLocation)\AppXManifest.xml" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}

Can be noisy — not the first choice.

Bulk re-registration touches every AppX package for the current user — noisy and usually not the first thing to try.

Common issue walkthrough

Start menu or taskbar broken after an update

  1. Identify the affected package, e.g. Get-AppxPackage Microsoft.Windows.StartMenuExperienceHost.
  2. Re-register just that package for the current user.
  3. Restart explorer.exe (or sign out/in) to reload the shell.
  4. If it persists, re-register all current-user AppX as a last resort.

New profile missing a provisioned app

  1. Check what's provisioned for new profiles: Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online.
  2. Re-provision the missing package if it was removed.
  3. Confirm the app appears the next time a new profile is created.

Blue Screen or Random Reboots
ProcessBlue Screen or Random Reboots
  1. Get the exact stop code from the blue screen if the user caught it, or pull it from the event log afterward.
  2. Ask about the pattern — under load (gaming, video calls), at random idle times, or right after waking from sleep?
  3. Check Reliability History and the System event log for BugCheck events around the reported times.
  4. Rule out a recent driver or Windows update installed right before the symptoms started.
  5. Run a memory diagnostic if the pattern is random and unexplained — bad RAM is a common silent cause.

Escalate when: the pattern correlates with a specific driver — try updating or rolling that driver back first; if it persists after that, it's a hardware dispatch, not a driver issue.

The exact stop code and the reliability history timeline are what actually narrow this down — guessing before checking those wastes the most time.

Get-WinEvent — Microsoft Learn ↗Stop error troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗ Bug check code reference — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Common issue walkthrough

Blue screen with a stop code

  1. Note the stop code and any file name shown.
  2. Boot normally or into Safe Mode and check Event Viewer and the crash dump.
  3. Roll back recent drivers or updates.
  4. Run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth.
  5. Test memory and disk if it keeps happening.

Random reboots with no blue screen

  1. Check Event Viewer for Kernel-Power 41.
  2. Check temperatures, power, and dust.
  3. Disable automatic restart to see the error.
  4. Update BIOS and drivers.
ResourcesStop error troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗Bug check code reference — Microsoft Learn ↗Windows Event Log — Microsoft Learn ↗
Can't Print
ProcessCan't Print
  1. Ask which printer, and whether it worked yesterday — this narrows a new problem from a longstanding one.
  2. Confirm the printer itself is powered on and shows no error on its own display.
  3. Ask if it's one user or several people printing to the same device.One user → check their PC's own print queue first.Several users → the problem is more likely the printer or print server, not any one PC.
  4. Have the user check for a stuck job in their own queue before touching the server.
  5. If the queue is clear but nothing prints, check network reachability to the printer's IP.

Escalate when: the printer's own display shows a paper jam or error but staff says it's physically clear — that's a sensor fault, treat it as a hardware ticket rather than continuing software troubleshooting.

Single-user vs. multi-user is the fork in the road for whether the PC or the print server is the actual problem.

Print troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗PrintManagement module — Microsoft Learn ↗ Test-NetConnection — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Common issue walkthrough

One user cannot print

  1. Confirm the right printer is selected and online.
  2. Clear the queue and restart the spooler.
  3. Remove and re-add the printer.

Nobody can print

  1. Check the print server or printer power and network.
  2. Restart the spooler on the server.
  3. Check the driver and recent updates.

Common issue walkthrough

Find a tool in the "CLI Tools" chapter

  1. Open the matching section below.
  2. Open the tool link and read its README or manual.
  3. Test it on a lab or non-production system first.
  4. Record what you used in the ticket or change note.
ResourcesCLI Tools chapter ↗Source list — GitHub ↗GNU Bash ↗
Common Symptom → Fix Path
ProcessComputer won't boot / stuck at logo
  1. Note exactly where it stalls (logo, spinning dots, blue screen, black screen) and any error code.
  2. Try a hard power cycle: hold power 10s, then restart.
  3. Boot into WinRE / Safe Mode if it won't reach the desktop.
  4. From WinRE: DISM /RestoreHealth, then sfc /scannow (see Windows Repair / Updates).
  5. After recovery, check Reliability/System events for the root cause (see Event Logs / Crash Investigation).
  6. Escalate to hardware diagnostics (RAM/disk test) if repair doesn't resolve it.

This is the standard order of operations for a boot failure — cheapest, least destructive steps first, hardware diagnostics last.

Windows Recovery Environment — Microsoft Learn ↗ Get-WinEvent — Microsoft Learn ↗ Troubleshoot Windows — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessNo internet access
  1. Confirm the adapter has a valid IP (see Networking / DNS / VPN / Wireless).
  2. Test a specific known-good destination on the actual port needed.
  3. Check DNS resolution separately from raw connectivity.
  4. If Wi-Fi, check signal/auth state: netsh wlan show interfaces.
  5. If it's site-wide, check the firewall/Meraki uplink before assuming it's one device (see Firewalls, Cisco Meraki).

This is the fast single-device pass — if it doesn't resolve it, or you're dealing with multiple devices, escalate to "Networking issue" (Escalation Decision Trees) for DHCP/APIPA and tracert-based diagnosis.

Splitting "can I reach anything" from "does DNS work" from "is Wi-Fi authenticated" narrows a vague complaint to one specific layer fast.

Test-NetConnection — Microsoft Learn ↗ Get-WinEvent — Microsoft Learn ↗ Troubleshoot Windows — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessApp won't open or keeps crashing
  1. Confirm no hung process from a prior session is blocking a new launch.
  2. Check the Application event log for the exact crash ID and faulting module (see Event Logs / Crash Investigation).
  3. For Office apps, try Quick Repair then Online Repair (see Office / Outlook).
  4. Check for a pending update or driver conflict introduced around the same time.
  5. Recreate the user profile only as a last resort if it's isolated to one profile.

The faulting-module name from the crash event is usually the single fastest way to tell a corrupt install apart from a driver conflict.

Get-WinEvent — Microsoft Learn ↗ Troubleshoot Windows — Microsoft Learn ↗ Microsoft Support ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessPrinter not printing
  1. Check for stuck jobs and clear them (see Printers / Spooler).
  2. Restart the print spooler service.
  3. Confirm the printer/driver is actually registered and reachable on the network.
  4. Reinstall the printer with the correct driver if the queue keeps corrupting.

This is the fast single-printer pass — for multiple users affected or a shared print server, escalate to "Printer & print server issue" (Escalation Decision Trees).

A corrupt driver causing repeat queue jams is the single most common root cause behind "printing worked yesterday" tickets.

Print troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗ Get-WinEvent — Microsoft Learn ↗ Troubleshoot Windows — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessSystem running slow
  1. Check CPU/RAM baseline (see Devices / Drivers / Hardware).
  2. Check free disk space — a nearly-full system drive is a very common slowdown cause (see VM & Storage Health).
  3. Check for a runaway process by CPU/working set.
  4. Confirm Windows Update isn't mid-install in the background.
  5. Check startup app load in Task Manager's Startup tab.

Disk space and startup bloat resolve more "slow computer" tickets than anything hardware-related — check those two before assuming it needs a rebuild.

Get-Process — Microsoft Learn ↗ Get-WinEvent — Microsoft Learn ↗ Troubleshoot Windows — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessCan't log in / forgot password
  1. Confirm lockout vs. genuinely wrong password (see Active Directory / Domain / Login).
  2. For AD accounts, unlock if locked out: Unlock-ADAccount.
  3. For a forgotten password, reset and force a change at next sign-in.
  4. For Entra/M365 accounts, confirm Conditional Access isn't blocking the sign-in location or device.

Lockout and "wrong password" look identical to the user but need different fixes — always confirm which one you're dealing with first.

Communication Systems
ProcessCall quality problems (choppy, echo, dropped calls)
  1. Ask: one user or many, wired or Wi-Fi, VPN or not, and what time.
  2. Check the headset or phone and test with another one.
  3. Move to wired Ethernet and close bandwidth-heavy apps.
  4. Check latency, jitter, and packet loss with ping -t and pathping.
  5. In Teams check Call Quality Dashboard / Call Analytics for that call.
  6. Check QoS and that required ports and endpoints are allowed through the firewall.
  7. If many users are affected, check the internet circuit and the voice/Teams service health.

Voice needs low latency (under ~150 ms), jitter (under ~30 ms), and packet loss (under ~1%). Most problems are Wi-Fi, VPN, or bandwidth.

Computer Won't Boot
ProcessComputer Won't Boot
  1. Ask the caller exactly what they see — a manufacturer logo that hangs, a black screen, a blue screen, or repeated restarts.Blue screen with a stop code → get the exact code before doing anything else. It points to the specific driver or hardware subsystem at fault.
  2. Confirm nothing changed recently — a Windows update, a new peripheral, or a recent power outage.
  3. Have them try a hard power cycle: hold the power button 10 seconds, unplug (and remove a removable battery) for 30 seconds, then power on.
  4. If it reaches Windows Recovery Environment automatically after repeated failures, walk them through Startup Repair.
  5. If you have remote or physical access, run the standard repair order: DISM /RestoreHealth then sfc /scannow.
  6. Reboot and confirm stability. Check Reliability History for repeat errors before closing the ticket.

Escalate when: it still won't boot after repair — this becomes a hardware/onsite dispatch case. Hand off to Escalation Decision Trees for the warranty-based routing.

Cheapest, least-destructive steps first — hardware diagnostics last. This mirrors the repair order used elsewhere in Windows Repair / Updates.

ProcessFind client documentation before starting a change

ProcessWhat to capture before escalating

ProcessWhen to escalate
  1. Risk of data loss if you proceed further
  2. Confirmed or suspected security incident (see Security Incident Response)
  3. Outage affecting multiple users or an entire site
  4. Requires vendor engagement (hardware warranty, licensed support)
  5. Exceeds your current access or change-authorization level

When in doubt on a security-flavored issue, escalate early — the cost of a false alarm is much lower than a missed compromise.

Clear escalation criteria reduce both under-escalation (sitting on a real incident too long) and over-escalation (routine tickets clogging a specialist queue).

Escalation Decision Trees
ProcessSoftware issue — supported vs. unsupported
  1. Check ticket history first — has this been worked before, and has a vendor already engaged?
  2. If it's software you support: try the least invasive fix first (clear cache, update OS/drivers).
  3. Check the vendor's own update/diagnostic tool before deeper troubleshooting (e.g. HP Image Assistant, Dell SupportAssist).
  4. Still unresolved? Open a ticket directly with Microsoft or the manufacturer.
  5. If it's software you don't support: contact the vendor directly rather than troubleshooting it yourself — coordinate admin access if they need it, and confirm resolution with the client before closing.

Knowing what you do and don't support up front saves time that would otherwise go into troubleshooting something outside your scope.

A clear supported/unsupported line prevents both under-delivering (giving up too early on something you should fix) and scope creep (spending hours on third-party software that isn't covered).

Microsoft 365 support resources — Microsoft Learn ↗ Print troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗ ITIL incident management — Atlassian ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessHardware & peripheral issue
  1. Check for a firmware/driver update from the manufacturer first.
  2. Get the exact error code before assuming a diagnosis.
  3. For peripherals: reseat cables, check for physical damage, and swap in a known-good unit to isolate the fault.
  4. Power-cycle (or a full power drain) before dispatching anyone onsite.
  5. Escalate onsite repair/replacement based on warranty status — in-warranty goes to the manufacturer or field service, out-of-warranty needs approval first.

Isolating whether it's the device, the cable, or the port (by swapping a known-good component) is usually faster than researching the exact error code first.

Warranty status determines the entire escalation path, so confirm it early — it changes whether you're routing to the manufacturer for free or needing billing approval first.

HP Image Assistant ↗ Print troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗ ITIL incident management — Atlassian ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessPrinter & print server issue
  1. Single user: ping the printer's IP, update drivers, restart the PC, and confirm the user's print codes/authorization on the device itself.
  2. Multiple users on one printer: reboot the printer and check its embedded web admin console for job/error logs before touching the print server.
  3. If it's the print server itself, restart it only with approval — it affects everyone printing through it.
  4. Rule out the underlying network before assuming it's the printer.

Single-user vs. multi-user is the fork in the road — it tells you whether to work the PC or the print server first. For a single user with no server involved, "Printer not printing" (Common Symptom → Fix Path) is the faster first pass.

Checking the printer's own embedded web admin console for job/error logs is often faster than guessing from symptoms alone, and works even when the print server is unreachable.

Print troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗ ITIL incident management — Atlassian ↗ Troubleshoot Windows — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessNetworking issue
  1. Single device: ping it, check DHCP, and run a tracert to see where the path breaks.
  2. Rule out DNS specifically: ipconfig /flushdns, and if you run a DNS security service (e.g. Cisco Umbrella), test with it temporarily disabled to isolate the cause.
  3. Multiple devices: an APIPA address (169.x.x.x) points straight to a DHCP problem — check the DHCP server/scope first.
  4. Tracert from the DC to a known-good external IP (e.g. 8.8.8.8) — the first hop is normally the internal gateway; the second or third is typically the first external hop.
  5. Confirm subnet/gateway settings on the DC, and check for a firewall IP that differs from the gateway.
  6. ISP issue: restart the modem/firewall before opening a ticket with the carrier.

An APIPA address on multiple devices at once is one of the most reliable single signals that DHCP — not the individual devices — is the actual problem. For a quicker first pass on a single device, start with "No internet access" (Common Symptom → Fix Path) instead.

Reading tracert hop-by-hop (internal gateway, then first external hop) pinpoints whether a break is inside your network or upstream at the ISP.

tracert — Microsoft Learn ↗ Print troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗ ITIL incident management — Atlassian ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessVM / RDP issue
  1. VM, single user: reboot the VM, then check for OS/VM version updates and update the user's network drivers.
  2. VM, multiple users: reboot the VM, check for OS/VM updates, and check host resource allocation/availability before assuming a software fault.
  3. RDP: verify the target address replies (ping/tracert), confirm the client is on the company network or VPN, and confirm Remote Desktop is actually enabled on the target device.

A VM problem affecting multiple users points toward the host (resources, updates) rather than any one guest OS — check host-level health before troubleshooting inside the VM.

Separating single-user from multi-user VM symptoms is the fastest way to tell a guest-OS problem apart from a host-level resource or update issue.

Restart-VM — Microsoft Learn ↗ Print troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗ ITIL incident management — Atlassian ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Common issue walkthrough

Picking the right decision tree for an ambiguous ticket

  1. Identify the category first — software, hardware, printer, network, or VM/RDP.
  2. If it spans more than one (e.g. "can't print over VPN"), work the networking tree first, since connectivity issues cascade into everything else.
  3. Follow the matching tree step by step rather than jumping straight to the escalation step.
  4. Note which path you followed in the ticket — it saves the next person from re-diagnosing from scratch.

Common issue walkthrough

App keeps crashing — need root cause

  1. Pull crash events (IDs 1000/1001) from the Application log for the relevant window.
  2. Cross-reference with any Windows Update or driver install around the same time.

Machine keeps rebooting unexpectedly

  1. Pull System log events for IDs 41/1074/6008.
  2. Look for a pattern — time of day, or correlation with scheduled tasks.
  3. Rule out a pending update or driver crash as the trigger.

First-Level Help Desk
ProcessTicket intake and priority
  1. Record who, what, when, how many affected, and the exact error.
  2. Set priority: P1 outage or data/security risk; P2 major function impaired; P3 single user or workaround exists; P4 request or question.
  3. Tell the user what to expect and when.
  4. Work in order of priority, then age.
  5. Update the ticket at each change and before you hand it off.
  6. Close with cause, fix, and how to prevent it.

A simple priority scheme and ticket routine.

ProcessVerify identity before resetting a password
  1. Use the approved method: call back to a number on file, manager approval, or the self-service portal.
  2. Never reset based only on an email or a chat message.
  3. Use a temporary password and force a change at next sign-in.
  4. Do not read passwords aloud or put them in the ticket.
  5. Record who was verified and how.

Password resets are a common social-engineering target, especially where PHI is stored.

No Internet / Can't Connect
ProcessNo Internet / Can't Connect
  1. Ask: is it one device, or is everyone in the office affected? This single question determines the entire rest of the call.One device → check adapter status and IP with the user directly.Everyone → check firewall/router status lights and the WAN uplink before touching any individual PC.
  2. Rule out DNS specifically by asking the user to try a raw IP address or a different site — if that works, it's DNS, not connectivity.
  3. If it's Wi-Fi, confirm they're actually on the corporate SSID and not a guest or neighboring network.
  4. Check whether a DNS security service (e.g. Cisco Umbrella) could be the block — test with it temporarily disabled if you can.
  5. For a site-wide outage, check the firewall/Meraki uplink status before opening a ticket with the carrier.

Escalate when: the outage is confirmed on the ISP side — stop troubleshooting internally, open a carrier ticket, and log the outage window for the client.

The single-vs-everyone question at the top of the call determines the entire rest of the diagnostic path.

Test-NetConnection — Microsoft Learn ↗Troubleshoot networking — Microsoft Learn ↗ ipconfig — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Common issue walkthrough

One device has no internet

  1. Check cable or Wi-Fi and the IP with ipconfig /all.
  2. Ping the gateway, then 8.8.8.8, then a name.
  3. Flush DNS and renew the IP.
  4. Reset the adapter or network stack if needed.

Everyone is offline

  1. Check the modem/firewall and ISP status.
  2. Check DHCP and DNS servers.
  3. Escalate to the ISP with the outage details.

Outlook / Email Problems
ProcessOutlook / Email Problems
  1. Ask exactly what's happening — not receiving mail, not sending, or a specific error message. Get the exact wording of any error.
  2. Confirm whether it's happening in Outlook only, or also on the web (outlook.office.com) — this tells you if it's a client problem or an account/service problem.Web works, desktop doesn't → client-side Outlook problem. Check for a hung process, then try a Quick Repair.Both broken → check Microsoft 365 Service Health first — this could be an outage, not a local fault.
  3. If mail isn't arriving from a specific sender, check the user's inbox rules and the tenant's spam/quarantine logs before assuming it's "just not arriving."
  4. Confirm resolution by having the user send and receive a real test message before closing the ticket.

Escalate when: inbox rules show signs of tampering (auto-forward/auto-delete the user didn't set up) — treat as a possible account compromise and move to Security Incident Response immediately.

Checking outlook.office.com separately from the desktop client is the fastest way to tell a client-side problem apart from a service-wide outage.

Microsoft 365 Service Health — Microsoft Learn ↗Outlook troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗ Microsoft 365 troubleshooting — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026

Print jobs stuck in queue

  1. List stuck jobs per printer: Get-PrintJob.
  2. Clear the stuck job(s): Remove-PrintJob.
  3. If that doesn't help, restart the spooler service.
  4. If it recurs, check the driver — corrupt drivers are a common repeat cause.

Printer missing or can't be added

  1. Confirm the printer and driver are actually registered.
  2. Check network reachability to the print server or device IP.
  3. Re-add the printer, installing the matching driver if missing.

Quick Fixes Before Escalating
Minor changeRestart the affected component
Restart-Service <ServiceName> -Force
# or, for the whole machine, once other options are exhausted
Restart-Computer

Restart the smallest thing that could fix it first — a service restart before a full reboot, a reboot before a reimage.

The classic first-pass fix — genuinely resolves a large share of transient issues and costs almost nothing to try.

Minor changeClear temp files & browser cache

Common issue walkthrough

Working through the quick-fix tier in order

  1. Try the least invasive fix first — a restart — before anything else.
  2. Move to cache/DNS resets if a restart doesn't clear it.
  3. Run the matching built-in troubleshooter if the cause is still unclear.
  4. If none of these clear it within a few minutes, stop guessing and escalate.

ProcessHealth plan and IT glossary
  1. PHI: protected health information. TPA: third-party administrator. BPaaS: business process as a service.
  2. MA / MAPD: Medicare Advantage (with Part D drugs). SNP: Special Needs Plan. Medicaid managed care: state-sponsored plan run by a health plan.
  3. CMS: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. HHS: Dept. of Health and Human Services.
  4. Adjudication: deciding how a claim is paid or denied. Remittance: payment explanation (835). EOB: Explanation of Benefits.
  5. Enrollment / eligibility: who is covered and when (834, 270/271).
  6. Encounter data: service records plans send to CMS or the state.
  7. NPI: National Provider Identifier. ICD-10 / CPT: diagnosis and procedure code sets.
  8. MFT: managed file transfer. SFTP: secure file transfer over SSH. PGP: file encryption.
  9. SPOF: single point of failure. RTO/RPO: how long to recover / how much data loss is acceptable.

Terms that come up daily when supporting health plan systems.

Common issue walkthrough

App won't uninstall cleanly

  1. Find its exact uninstall string in the registry Uninstall key.
  2. Try the vendor's silent switch first.
  3. If that fails, try winget uninstall.
  4. As a last resort, manually clean leftover registry/folder remnants and document what was removed.

Service won't start or crashes repeatedly

  1. Check current status and last error via Get-Service and the Service Control Manager event log.
  2. Try a manual restart: Restart-Service -Force.
  3. If it won't start, check the account it runs as and the permissions it needs.
  4. Confirm dependent services aren't also down.

assign letter=Z
exit

bcdboot C:\Windows /s Z: /f UEFI
bcdedit /set {bootmgr} device partition=Z:
bcdedit /set {bootmgr} path \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi
bcdedit

Disable BitLocker before starting. Reboot and confirm the system boots normally before cleaning up the old EFI partition.

Rebuilds the EFI boot partition on a UEFI system — needed when the original ESP is missing, corrupted, or needs to move to make room for a repartition.

Big changeRecreate the recovery partition (WinRE)
reagentc /info
# if a recovery partition already exists but is unregistered, point WinRE at it:
reagentc /setreimage /path R:\Recovery\WindowsRE
reagentc /enable

# if the partition itself needs to be (re)created — GPT disks:
diskpart
select disk X
select partition Y        # the new/target recovery partition
set id=de94bba4-06d1-4d40-a16a-bfd50179d6ac
gpt attributes=0x8000000000000001
exit

Leave at least 1GB free at the end of the disk before creating the partition. If WinRE.wim is still present under C:\Windows\System32\Recovery, you don't need to source it from install media.

reagentc /info tells you immediately whether WinRE is enabled and where it's pointed — always check this first before assuming the partition itself is the problem.

Minor changeWindows Update button is greyed out
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate"
# set SetDisableUXWUAccess from 1 to 0, then restart the Update service or reboot
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate" /v SetDisableUXWUAccess /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

This policy value is what greys out the "Check for updates" button in Settings — usually left over from a GPO that no longer applies, or a manual restriction someone forgot to remove.

A single registry value under the WindowsUpdate policy key controls whether the update UI is interactive — flipping it back to 0 restores the button without touching any other update settings.

Common issue walkthrough

System unstable or corrupted after an update

  1. Run DISM /CheckHealth then /ScanHealth to assess corruption.
  2. Run DISM /RestoreHealth to repair the component store.
  3. Run sfc /scannow to repair protected files from the restored store.
  4. Reboot and check reliability history for repeat errors.

Updates stuck or failing to install

  1. Generate the update log: Get-WindowsUpdateLog.
  2. Check for a pending reboot blocking new installs.
  3. If updates are stuck, stop wuauserv, rename the SoftwareDistribution folder, and restart the service.
  4. Retry Windows Update and monitor the new log.

02 NetworkingMeraki, switching and VLANs, VPN, DNS, wireless, firewalls, Auvik topology mapping, and network data flows
Auvik & Network Topology Management
ProcessHow Auvik works (data flow)
  1. A lightweight collector (Windows service, OVA, Docker, or bash install) runs on the customer network.
  2. It discovers devices with SNMP, WMI, and ICMP, and maps connections with LLDP, CDP, and forwarding tables.
  3. Data goes securely to the Auvik cloud, which builds interactive maps and inventory.
  4. Alerts for new devices and critical changes can create tickets in your PSA.
  5. Device configs are backed up when added or changed, with version history and compare.

The pieces of Auvik and how data moves. Auvik is a network monitoring and topology tool commonly used by MSPs.

Auvik network discovery ↗ Auvik network mapping ↗ Auvik automated documentation ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessData flow — what a clean small-business topology map should show
  1. Every device should appear once and connect to the device above it; unexpected links can mean a loop or a rogue switch.
  2. Check that uplinks match the design (speed, trunk, redundancy).
  3. Look for unknown devices and unmanaged switches; add or remove them from the map as appropriate.
  4. Compare the live map to the documented diagram after every change.
  5. Save the diagram as evidence for audits and onboarding.

Reading a map: what normal looks like and what to question.

Network topology — Wikipedia ↗ Auvik network mapping ↗ Network design basics — Cisco ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessSet up Auvik for a new site
  1. Create the site in Auvik and download the collector for your platform.
  2. Install the collector on a server or VM at the site (or import the OVA).
  3. Enter discovery credentials: SNMP (v2c or v3), WMI/domain account, and device SSH or CLI logins where needed.
  4. Confirm the collector shows online and devices begin to appear in the map.
  5. Name and tag devices, set the device roles, and confirm each important switch and firewall is monitored (not just discovered).
  6. Turn on config backup and set alert recipients and PSA integration.

Use read-only SNMP credentials wherever possible and store credentials in your password manager.

A repeatable site onboarding checklist for Auvik.

Auvik support center ↗ Auvik network discovery ↗ SNMP — Wikipedia ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessAuvik device not showing or shown as unmanaged
  1. Confirm the collector is online and has network access to the device's VLAN.
  2. Check SNMP is enabled on the device, the community or v3 user matches, and the collector's IP is allowed.
  3. For Windows servers, confirm the WMI account and firewall rules.
  4. Check the credentials are assigned to the right site and device.
  5. Review the device's discovery status and errors in Auvik.
  6. Rerun discovery or rescan after fixing and confirm the status changes to monitored.

The usual reasons a device is discovered but not fully managed.

Auvik support center ↗ SNMP — Wikipedia ↗ Troubleshoot SNMP — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessAuvik map shows wrong or missing links
  1. Check that LLDP or CDP is enabled on both ends of the link.
  2. Confirm both devices are managed and have valid credentials.
  3. Check for unmanaged switches in the path, which hide connections.
  4. Wait for a full discovery cycle after a change, then refresh the map.
  5. Compare to the switch's own neighbor table (show lldp neighbors or show cdp neighbors).
  6. Fix the device config, not the map, when they disagree.

Maps are built from what devices report, so wrong maps usually mean device-side settings.

Auvik network mapping ↗ LLDP — Wikipedia ↗ LLDP and CDP — Cisco ↗ Checked Jul 2026

ProcessUse Auvik for change and incident work
  1. Before a change: save the current map and config as the baseline.
  2. During: watch the map and alerts for the affected devices.
  3. After: compare the new config to the previous version and check the map matches the plan.
  4. For an outage: find the offline device on the map, check upstream devices first, then the link between them.
  5. Add the result and screenshots to the ticket and update the client documentation.

Turns the topology map into a troubleshooting and change-control tool.

ProcessTopology management tools and alternatives
  1. Auvik: cloud network discovery, maps, monitoring, and config backup for MSPs.
  2. Meraki Dashboard: built-in topology for Meraki-only networks.
  3. PRTG, SolarWinds, LogicMonitor, Zabbix: monitoring with network maps.
  4. NetBox: source-of-truth inventory and IP management (documentation, not discovery).
  5. Draw.io, Lucidchart, Visio: hand-drawn diagrams for design and documentation.
  6. Rule: use discovery for what exists now and diagrams for what you intended.

Choose by need: discovery and monitoring, inventory, or design drawings.

ProcessData flow — Meraki cloud management vs local data path
  1. Devices connect out to the Meraki cloud over HTTPS to download configuration and report status.
  2. User traffic does not go through the cloud; it moves across the local switches, access points, and MX.
  3. If the internet is down, the network keeps working locally but you cannot change settings from the dashboard.
  4. A device showing offline in the dashboard usually has lost its uplink, DNS, or access to the Meraki cloud.
  5. Check the device's local status page (when reachable) and the dashboard event log.

Why Meraki sites keep running during a dashboard outage, and what "offline" means.

Common issue walkthrough

Site down — need root cause fast

  1. Check WAN uplink status first.
  2. Check device status for the specific MX/switch/AP.
  3. Check the client connectivity list to see if devices are even associating.
  4. Reboot the device only if status confirms it's hung, not just an uplink/ISP issue.

New AP not appearing or clients can't connect

  1. Confirm the device was claimed into the right network in the dashboard.
  2. Check device status via the API for adoption/online state.
  3. Check the client list to confirm at least some devices are associating.

Cisco Switching (VLANs)
SafeCisco IOS/IOS-XECheck VLAN & port status
show vlan
show interface status

show vlan lists every VLAN and which ports are assigned to it; show interface status gives a one-line-per-port summary (connected/notconnect, speed/duplex, assigned VLAN) — usually the faster of the two for a "why can't this port reach the network" call.

The standard first check before touching any switch config — confirms both what VLANs exist and which physical ports are actually up and assigned where you expect.

Cisco Catalyst 9300 command references ↗ Cisco support ↗ Cisco Learning Network ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Minor changeCisco IOS/IOS-XEConfigure a switch port's VLAN
configure terminal
interface range gi1/0/24
switchport access vlan <vlan-ID>
switchport mode access
auto qos trust
exit

interface range lets you apply the same config to multiple ports at once (e.g. interface range gi1/0/1-24). auto qos trust is optional — only relevant if you're trusting QoS markings from the connected device (like a VoIP phone).

The standard sequence for moving a port onto a specific VLAN — confirm the VLAN already exists (show vlan) before assigning a port to it, since assigning to a nonexistent VLAN silently creates it.

Cisco IOS interface commands reference ↗ Cisco Catalyst 9300 command reference ↗ Cisco support ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessData flow — VLANs, trunks, and inter-VLAN routing
  1. Each VLAN is a separate broadcast domain; access ports carry one VLAN untagged.
  2. The trunk between switches carries many VLANs tagged with 802.1Q; both ends must allow the same VLANs and native VLAN.
  3. A device in one VLAN reaches another VLAN only through a router or L3 switch (the VLAN's gateway address).
  4. Check with show vlan brief, show interfaces trunk, and show ip interface brief.
  5. Wrong VLAN on a port or a missing VLAN on a trunk is the most common cause of one-device-cannot-connect.

How VLANs, trunks, and the L3 gateway fit together.

VLAN basics — Cisco ↗ IEEE 802.1Q overview — Wikipedia ↗ Cisco IOS command reference ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Common issue walkthrough

Device on the wrong VLAN

  1. Check port status and VLAN with show vlan brief and show interfaces status.
  2. Confirm the port mode (access or trunk).
  3. Set the correct access VLAN and save the config.

Trunk or VLAN not passing traffic

  1. Check show interfaces trunk for allowed VLANs.
  2. Confirm the VLAN exists on both switches.
  3. Check native VLAN matches on both ends.

ProcessData flow — firewall packet path
  1. The packet enters a zone or interface and is matched against rules top to bottom; the first match wins.
  2. If allowed, security profiles (IPS, antivirus, URL filtering) may inspect it.
  3. NAT and routing decide where it goes next.
  4. Anything with no matching allow rule is dropped and should be logged.
  5. To troubleshoot, find the log entry for the source, destination, and port and read which rule matched.

The order a firewall evaluates traffic. Knowing it tells you where to look in the logs.

NIST SP 800-41 firewall guidelines ↗ Firewall logs best practices — NIST SP 800-92 ↗ Network security groups — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Common issue walkthrough

Site can't reach an external service

  1. Check session state at the firewall (PAN: show session all filter / Forti: diagnose sys session filter).
  2. Confirm the relevant policy is actually matching.
  3. Clear a stuck session if the policy looks correct but traffic still fails.
  4. Rule out DNS resolution as the actual root cause before assuming it's the firewall.

VPN or NAT rule stopped working after a change

  1. Compare current config against last known-good, if you have config versioning.
  2. Check policy order — a broader rule above the intended one can shadow it.
  3. Test with a scoped rule change before rolling out broadly.

ProcessReset network settings (Windows 11)
  1. Open Settings > Network & Internet > Advanced network settings.
  2. Select Network reset, then Reset now.
  3. Confirm. The PC restarts and network adapters are reinstalled.
  4. Reconnect to Wi-Fi and re-add any VPN profiles.

ProcessData flow — hybrid DNS (on-prem and Azure)
  1. On-prem clients ask the on-prem DNS server.
  2. For Azure private names, a conditional forwarder sends the query to the Private Resolver inbound endpoint.
  3. The resolver answers from the linked Private DNS zone.
  4. Azure VMs use the outbound endpoint with forwarding rules to resolve on-prem names.
  5. Test both directions with nslookup name server-ip from each side.

Two-way name resolution between a local network and Azure.

Common issue walkthrough

Intermittent connectivity or can't reach a server

  1. Confirm the adapter is up with a valid IP: Get-NetAdapter, Get-NetIPConfiguration.
  2. Test the specific port: Test-NetConnection -Port.
  3. Check DNS is resolving correctly: Resolve-DnsName.
  4. Clear the DNS cache and retest: Clear-DnsClientCache.

Wi-Fi drops repeatedly

  1. Check current signal/state: netsh wlan show interfaces.
  2. Check adapter power-saving settings — "allow the computer to turn off this device" is a common culprit.
  3. Update or roll back the Wi-Fi driver if the pattern correlates with a recent update.

SMTP Test (Telnet)
ProcessTest SMTP manually with Telnet
  1. Enable the Telnet Client Windows feature if needed.
  2. Run telnet <servername> 25.
  3. Type EHLO test.com — expect 250.
  4. Type MAIL FROM:admin@test.com — expect 250.
  5. Type RCPT TO:user@domain.com — expect 250.
  6. Type DATA — expect 354.
  7. Type a subject and message, press Enter twice, then . on its own line — expect 250.
  8. Type QUIT — expect 221.
  9. Confirm the recipient received it; on errors check the server event/transport logs.

Walks through an SMTP conversation by hand to prove a server accepts and relays mail on the chosen port.

ProcessData flow — remote access VPN
  1. The client builds an encrypted tunnel to the gateway.
  2. The gateway checks credentials with RADIUS, Entra ID, or AD (and MFA if required).
  3. Allowed routes decide what the user can reach: split tunnel (only company ranges) or full tunnel (everything).
  4. If connected but nothing works, check DNS settings, routes, and firewall rules for the VPN pool.
  5. If it will not connect, check credentials, MFA, certificate, and whether UDP 500/4500 or the SSL port is blocked.

Common issue walkthrough

User can't connect to VPN

  1. Check the client-side profile status: Get-VpnConnection.
  2. Try reconnecting: rasdial.
  3. If the profile looks broken, recreate it: Add-VpnConnection.
  4. Check the concentrator side for a matching session attempt — if it's not arriving, the issue is upstream.

Site-to-site tunnel down

  1. Check phase-1 status (ASA: show crypto isakmp sa, or the Meraki VPN status endpoint).
  2. Confirm the peer's public IP hasn't changed.
  3. Check the pre-shared key or certificate hasn't expired.
  4. Re-initiate the tunnel and monitor for phase-1/phase-2 establishment.

Common issue walkthrough

User can't log in / account locked

  1. Confirm lockout state: Get-ADUser -Properties LockedOut,BadLogonCount.

Group membership isn't granting expected access

  1. Confirm actual membership: Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership.

Application Infrastructure & Tracing
ProcessTrace a failing application end to end
  1. Write the chain: user > network/VPN > DNS > web tier > application tier > database > file/batch feeds.
  2. Test DNS: nslookup server.
  3. Test the port: Test-NetConnection server -Port 443 (Windows) or nc -zv server 443 (Unix).
  4. Test the service: curl -vk https://server/ or open it in the browser and check the status code.
  5. Check the service and its logs on the server.
  6. Test the database from the app server.
  7. Check disk, CPU, and memory.
  8. Check what changed recently: patch, deployment, certificate, password, schedule.

Application infrastructure problems are solved by checking one link at a time.

ProcessCommon application tiers and ports

  3. SQL Server: 1433. Db2: 50000 (common default). Oracle: 1521. MySQL: 3306. PostgreSQL: 5432.
  4. DNS: 53. LDAP: 389. LDAPS: 636. Kerberos: 88. SMB: 445. RDP: 3389.
  5. SMTP: 25, 587 (submission), 465 (SMTPS). Confirm real ports in the environment documentation.

ProcessData flow — hybrid three-tier app (Azure front end, on-prem database)
  1. Users reach the public front door (gateway and web firewall), which sends traffic to the web and app tier.
  2. The app tier talks to the on-prem database over the private VPN or ExpressRoute link; the database is never exposed to the internet.
  3. Latency across the link affects every query, so keep chatty calls and large result sets in mind.
  4. To trace a slow request, time each hop: browser, gateway, app, link, database.
  5. Use correlation IDs in logs so one request can be followed through every tier.

A common hybrid layout and the hops to measure when tracing a slow or failing request.

Batch Jobs & Scheduling
ProcessMonitor production batch jobs
  1. Open the scheduler console (for example ROC Maestro, cron, or Task Scheduler) at the start of your shift.
  2. Check each job stream: finished, running late, failed, or waiting on a dependency.
  3. For anything failed or late, open the job log and note the error and time.
  4. Check disk space and the database/server the job depends on.
  5. Report failures to the owner with the job name, time, and error text.
  6. Log the result in the ticket or shift notes.

A simple checklist for daily monitoring; names differ by scheduler but the steps are the same.

ProcessA batch job failed — triage order
  1. Capture the job name, run time, and exit code.
  2. Read the end of the job log first, then work backward to the first error.
  3. Check usual causes: input file missing/late, disk full, locked table, expired password, network or server down, dependency job failed.
  4. If the fix is safe and documented, correct it and rerun (or release) the job.
  5. If not, hold dependent jobs and escalate.
  6. Document the cause and the fix.

Most batch failures are caused by missing inputs, space, locks, or credentials.

ProcessData flow — scheduled batch job stream
  1. The scheduler starts a job stream at its run time once its dependencies are met (files present, previous streams done).
  2. Jobs run in order; each starts only when the one before it succeeds.
  3. A failure stops the chain and alerts the operator.
  4. On failure: read the job output, fix the cause, then rerun from the failed job rather than the whole stream, if your procedure allows.
  5. Record the cause and the rerun in the ticket.

How a scheduled chain of jobs behaves, and how to respond when one fails.

ProcessLook up any Group Policy setting (GPS tool)
  1. Open the Group Policy Search tool and type a keyword (e.g. "Windows Update", "BitLocker", "USB storage").
  2. Use the product filter to narrow results to the OS/Office version you're targeting.
  3. Click a result to see its full details: Setting Type, Supported On, registry Key/Value, and the ADMX file it comes from.
  4. Toggle Registry View to jump straight to the exact HKLM/HKCU path and value — useful when scripting the equivalent registry change.
  5. Use Share > Registry Key+Value (or Category Path) to copy a direct link/reference for a ticket or runbook.
  6. Grab the current ADMX templates from the Link to ADMX Download if you need to import new policy definitions into your central store.

Covers every documented Group Policy setting across Windows and Office versions, including deprecated ones — useful both for finding a setting by keyword and for reverse-engineering what registry key a known policy actually writes.

Faster than digging through GPMC by hand when you know roughly what you're looking for but not the exact policy path — the Registry View feature is especially handy when you need the raw key/value to replicate a setting outside of Group Policy (e.g. in an Intune settings catalog or a script).

ProcessData flow — on-prem domain logon (DHCP, DNS, Kerberos, GPO)
  1. The PC gets an IP address and DNS server from DHCP (DNS must point at AD DNS, not the router).
  2. It asks DNS for the domain controller records.
  3. It authenticates to the DC with Kerberos (time must be within 5 minutes).
  4. Group Policy downloads from SYSVOL and applies; drive maps and scripts run.
  5. Most logon problems are DNS, time, or network path: check those before the account.

The order of events at logon, so you can tell which layer is failing (network, DNS, time, authentication, policy).

Common issue walkthrough

GPO not applying to some machines

  1. Confirm the GPO is linked/enabled at the right OU: Get-GPInheritance.
  2. Check the target machine's applied policy: gpresult /h report.html.
  3. Force a refresh: Invoke-GPUpdate -Computer <name> -Force.
  4. Check SYSVOL replication isn't lagging on the DC serving that site.

AD replication errors between sites

  1. Get an overview: repadmin /replsummary.
  2. Drill into failing partners: repadmin /showrepl on the affected DC.
  3. Check network connectivity/firewall rules between sites — AD needs several ports open.
  4. Re-run dcdiag /v after fixing connectivity to confirm resolution.

Common issue walkthrough

User denied access to a shared folder

  1. Check effective NTFS permissions: icacls or Get-Acl.
  2. Check the separate share-level permission: Get-SmbShareAccess.
  3. Grant the missing right at whichever layer is restrictive.
  4. Have the user disconnect and reconnect the mapped drive to refresh the token.

Running out of space on a file server volume

  1. Find the largest files/folders sorted by size.
  2. Check for recent large writes via LastWriteTime.
  3. Move, archive, or extend the volume as appropriate (see VM & Storage Health).
  4. Set up a space-alert threshold going forward if none exists.

ProcessFortra GoAnywhereCommon transfer failure causes
  1. Connection timed out: firewall or IP allow-list change.
  2. Authentication failed: expired password or wrong/rotated SSH key.
  3. Host key changed: partner server was rebuilt; verify with them before accepting.

  5. No file found: partner did not send yet, or file name pattern changed.

ProcessFortra GoAnywhereOnboard a new SFTP trading partner

ProcessData flow — managed file transfer with GoAnywhere

HEALTHsuite (RAM Platform)
ProcessHow HEALTHsuite fits together
  1. HEALTHsuite is RAM's own platform for managing health plan client data. Users work in a browser (HTML pages); the pages read and write data in a SQL database.
  2. Chain to remember: user's browser > network > web/application server > database (SQL) > batch jobs and file feeds (GoAnywhere, Maestro) that load and extract data.
  3. A problem can sit in any link, so test them one at a time starting at the user and working back.
  4. Data usually enters through scheduled file loads and leaves through extracts and reports.
  5. Everything touching it is regulated PHI — handle it under HIPAA rules.

Confirm the specific tiers, servers and tables from RAM's internal documentation.

A mental model for supporting a browser-based application that sits on a database. This is a general model; the internal design is documented in RAM's own runbooks.

ProcessA HEALTHsuite page will not load or errors
  1. Ask: which page, which user, what time, and the exact message. Does it fail for everyone or one user?
  2. Try another browser or a private window; hard refresh with Ctrl+F5.
  3. Open developer tools (F12) > Network and reload; note the failing request and its HTTP status.
  4. Status guide: 401/403 permissions or session; 404 wrong or missing page; 500 application or database error; 502/503/504 web or app tier down or slow.
  5. If 500 or 5xx, check the application and web server logs for the same time.
  6. Test the database from the app server (see test connection).
  7. If everyone is affected, check the web/app services and the database before anything else.
  8. Escalate with URL, time, user, status code, and log lines.

Following the request from the browser backward finds the failing layer quickly.

ProcessReply to a health plan customer technical question
  1. Acknowledge quickly: you have it, who owns it, and when they will hear back.
  2. Restate the question in one sentence to confirm you understood.
  3. Gather facts: what, when, who affected, screenshots or IDs (no PHI in email).

  5. Give a next update time, even if the answer is "still investigating".
  6. Log the question, answer, and resolution so the next person can reuse it.

ROC Maestro
ProcessROC MaestroMaestro vocabulary and job states
  1. Workstation (CPU): a server or agent where jobs run.
  2. Job: one unit of work (a script or command).
  3. Job stream (schedule): a group of jobs with dependencies and a run window.
  4. Dependency: what a job waits on — another job, a file, a time, or a resource.
  5. Limit: how many jobs may run at once on a workstation or stream.
  6. Fence: jobs with a priority below the fence will not launch.
  7. Common states: SUCC (finished OK), ABEND (failed), FAIL (could not launch), EXEC (running), READY (can launch), WAIT (waiting on dependencies), HOLD (held by an operator), PEND/SCHED (waiting for the stream start).

ROC Maestro descends from the original Maestro scheduler (later Tivoli/HCL Workload Scheduler). The conman commands here follow that lineage; confirm exact syntax in your version.

Maestro schedulers share a common model. Learn these words first; every command and screen uses them.

ROC Maestro for Open Systems overview ↗ conman commands — HCL Workload Automation ↗ Maestro UNIX user guide (Tivoli lineage) — Princeton archive ↗ Checked Jul 2026
SafeROC MaestroSee jobs and job streams (showjobs / showschedules)
conman "sj"                      # show jobs (short form of showjobs)
conman "sj @#@.@"                # all jobs on all workstations
conman "sj @#@.@" | grep -i abend   # only failed jobs
conman "ss @"                    # show job streams
conman "ss @#STREAMNAME"        # one stream

sj and ss are read-only. Use them first thing in the morning and again when a user reports a late or missing file.

conman commands — HCL Workload Automation ↗ Maestro UNIX user guide (Tivoli lineage) — Princeton archive ↗ ROC Maestro for Open Systems overview ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Minor changeROC MaestroRerun a failed job
conman "sj @#STREAMNAME.@"          # find the exact name and state
conman "rr WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.JOBNAME"   # rerun (short for rerun)

Confirm the job is safe to rerun (some jobs duplicate data if run twice).

Reruns a job that ended in ABEND after the cause is fixed. Check dependent jobs and whether the job is safe to repeat.

conman commands — HCL Workload Automation ↗ Maestro UNIX user guide (Tivoli lineage) — Princeton archive ↗ ROC Maestro for Open Systems overview ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Minor changeROC MaestroRelease, hold, and confirm
conman "rj WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.JOBNAME"      # release job dependencies
conman "rs WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME"              # release a stream
conman "conf WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.JOBNAME ;succ"   # confirm as successful
conman "conf WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.JOBNAME ;abend"  # confirm as failed

release lets a held or waiting job proceed; confirm marks the result of a job that was run manually outside Maestro.

conman commands — HCL Workload Automation ↗ Maestro UNIX user guide (Tivoli lineage) — Princeton archive ↗ ROC Maestro for Open Systems overview ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Big changeROC MaestroCancel or kill a job
conman "cj WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.JOBNAME"   # cancel (job will not run)
conman "k  WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.JOBNAME"   # kill a running job

Get approval and tell the owner — dependent jobs can be skipped or blocked.

cancel removes a job from the day's run; kill stops one that is executing. Downstream jobs may be affected.

conman commands — HCL Workload Automation ↗ Maestro UNIX user guide (Tivoli lineage) — Princeton archive ↗ ROC Maestro for Open Systems overview ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Minor changeROC MaestroAdd or remove a dependency
conman "adj WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.JOBNAME ;follows WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.OTHERJOB"
conman "ddj WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.JOBNAME ;follows WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.OTHERJOB"

Changes affect today's run only. Document the reason in the ticket.

Temporarily make a job wait for another one, or remove a dependency that is blocking it.

Minor changeROC MaestroSubmit an ad hoc job or command
conman "sbd 'ls -l /data/inbound'"            # submit a command
conman "sbj JOBNAME"                          # submit an existing job
conman "sbs STREAMNAME"                       # submit a stream

Runs something now outside the normal plan. Useful for testing or catching up.

Minor changeROC MaestroLimit, fence, and priority
conman "lc WORKSTATION ;5"               # job limit on a workstation
conman "ls WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME ;3"    # job limit on a stream
conman "f 20"                            # set the fence (jobs below 20 will not launch)
conman "ap WORKSTATION#STREAMNAME.JOBNAME ;10"   # change job priority

Controls how many jobs run at once and which run first. Use when the system is overloaded or a priority job is stuck behind others.

Big changeROC MaestroStart and stop production processes
conman "stop"
conman "stop ;progressive"
conman "start"

Never stop production processes without approval — it pauses all scheduled work on that machine.

Starts or stops the scheduler's production processes on a workstation. Jobs on that workstation will not launch while stopped.

ProcessROC MaestroA job abended — what to do
  1. Run conman "sj" and note the job name, stream, workstation, and time.
  2. Open the job's output/log (path is in the job definition) and read the end first.
  3. Check the usual causes: input file missing, filesystem full, database error (SQLCODE), expired password, remote host down.
  4. Check downstream jobs that are waiting on it.
  5. Fix the cause. If safe, rerun with rr; if not, hold dependents and escalate.
  6. Document the cause, fix, and time in the ticket.

The quickest path from alert to cause for a failed batch job.

conman commands — HCL Workload Automation ↗ Maestro UNIX user guide (Tivoli lineage) — Princeton archive ↗ ROC Maestro for Open Systems overview ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Common issue walkthrough

Nightly stream abended

  1. Run conman "sj @#@.@" | grep -i abend.
  2. Read the job log, fix the cause (space, file, database).
  3. conman "rr <job>" if safe to rerun.
  4. Release dependents and report.

A job is stuck in WAIT or HOLD

  1. conman "sj" shows what it follows.
  2. Check whether the predecessor finished or the file exists.
  3. rj to release, or ddj to remove the dependency, with approval.

Common issue walkthrough

VM disk-full alert

  1. Check guest-level free space: Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk.
  2. If the guest disk has room on the underlying disk, extend the partition: Resize-Partition.
  3. If the underlying disk is also full, grow it first (Azure disk, Hyper-V VHD, or VMware datastore).
  4. Clean up large/old files as a stopgap while the resize is scheduled.

Host storage full even though guests report free space

  1. Check dynamic VHD/VHDX actual file size vs. configured max: Get-VHD.
  2. Check for orphaned snapshots/checkpoints consuming space.
  3. Compact or consolidate disks during a maintenance window.

Change Management for Automation (On-Prem / Hybrid / Cloud)
ProcessChange request: what to include
  1. Summary: what is changing and why.
  2. Systems and users affected, and the risk and impact.
  3. Type: standard (pre-approved), normal (needs review), or emergency.
  4. Implementation steps, who does them, and the schedule/window.
  5. Test plan and how success will be verified.
  6. Backout (rollback) plan and the point of no return.
  7. Approvals and communication plan.
  8. Post-change review: did it work, what was learned.

A complete change record makes approval faster and recovery easier.

Change management — Atlassian ↗ NIST SP 800-128 configuration management ↗ ITIL change enablement — Atlassian ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessRoll out a new automation or AI agent safely
  1. Pilot in a test environment or with one low-risk client or team.
  2. Start in approval-required mode — a person confirms every action.
  3. Review the audit log of what it did and what it would have done.
  4. Fix gaps in rules, permissions, and data.
  5. Widen to more clients in stages, still with approval on risky actions.
  6. Move low-risk, proven tasks to zero-touch; keep approval on access changes, deletions, and anything affecting PHI.
  7. Schedule regular reviews and keep a rollback plan and kill switch.

The same staged approach works for Pia automations, Thread flows, Power Automate, and in-house scripts.

Change management — Atlassian ↗ NIST AI Risk Management Framework ↗ Pia pre-built automations ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessOn-prem, hybrid, or cloud: what changes
  1. Identity: on-prem uses Active Directory; cloud uses Entra ID; hybrid needs sync (Entra Connect) and care with which side owns an object.
  2. Connectivity: on-prem and hybrid automations often need an agent or connector inside the network and outbound firewall rules.
  3. Credentials: service accounts and permissions differ by side — least privilege on both.
  4. Data location: confirm where data is processed and stored, especially PHI.
  5. Updates: on-prem you patch the agent; cloud the vendor does.
  6. Failure modes: a hybrid link, DNS, or certificate problem can break the automation even if both sides are healthy.
  7. Testing: test on-prem and cloud paths separately and together.

Where the work runs changes the permissions, network, and failure points you must plan for.

NIST SP 800-128 configuration management ↗ Microsoft Entra Connect — Microsoft Learn ↗ Change management — Atlassian ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessEmergency change and rollback
  1. Declare it an emergency change and notify the approver.
  2. Record what you are doing and why, in real time.
  3. Take a backup or snapshot if time allows.
  4. Make the smallest change that restores service.
  5. Verify service and tell the stakeholders.
  6. Do the full change record and review afterward.

When something is down, act fast but keep a record. The review afterward is where the process improves.

Change management — Atlassian ↗ NIST SP 800-128 configuration management ↗ Incident management — Atlassian ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessPost-change checklist
  1. Confirm the change works and nothing else broke.
  2. Check monitoring, logs, and scheduled jobs.
  3. Update documentation and runbooks.
  4. Close the change record with results and lessons.
  5. Tell users and stakeholders it is done.

Closing the loop keeps documentation and monitoring accurate.

Change management — Atlassian ↗ NIST SP 800-128 configuration management ↗ ITIL change enablement — Atlassian ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Common issue walkthrough

Rolling out a new automation

  1. Write the change request.
  2. Pilot in test with approval on every action.
  3. Review the audit log and widen in stages.
  4. Move proven low-risk tasks to zero-touch.

Moving an automation from on-prem to cloud

  1. List identity, network, and credential dependencies.
  2. Build and test the cloud version in parallel.
  3. Cut over in a window with a rollback plan.
  4. Verify, then retire the old one.

ProcessOn-prem Exchange vs Microsoft 365 — which admin portal
  1. On-prem mailbox: manage in the Exchange admin center at https://<server>/ecp and use OWA on the server URL.
  2. Cloud mailbox: manage in the Microsoft 365 / Exchange admin center and sign in via office.com.
  3. Check which one applies: Get-Mailbox in Exchange Online returns it only if it is a cloud mailbox.
  4. Hybrid: recipients live in one place; edit them in the portal that owns the mailbox.

ProcessData flow — Exchange hybrid mail flow
  1. Mail from the internet reaches Exchange Online Protection first (if the MX record points to Microsoft).
  2. Exchange Online delivers to cloud mailboxes, or routes to on-prem for mailboxes that still live there.
  3. The hybrid send and receive connectors carry mail between the two sides over TLS; the certificate must be valid and match.
  4. Check message trace in the Exchange admin center to see where a message stopped.
  5. Outbound mail from on-prem can route through Exchange Online if centralized mail transport is enabled.

Common issue walkthrough

External mail bouncing or not delivering

  1. Confirm the domain accepts mail: Get-AcceptedDomain.
  2. Trace the specific message: Get-MessageTraceV2.
  3. Check for a transport rule silently redirecting or blocking it: Get-TransportRule.
  4. Verify the outbound connector/smart host: Get-SendConnector.
  5. If hybrid, confirm hybrid config is healthy: Get-HybridConfiguration.

Hybrid mail flow breaks after a change

  1. Review the full hybrid config: Get-HybridConfiguration | fl *.
  2. Check both connector directions: Get-InboundConnector / Get-OutboundConnector.
  3. Confirm the outbound public IP hasn't changed: nslookup myip.opendns.com resolver1.opendns.com.
  4. Re-run the Hybrid Configuration Wizard if connector settings look stale.

ProcessFolder permission levels (what each one allows)
  1. Owner: full control including permissions.
  2. PublishingEditor: create, edit, delete all items and subfolders.
  3. Editor: create, edit, delete all items.
  4. PublishingAuthor: create items and subfolders; edit/delete own items.
  5. Author: create items; edit/delete own items.
  6. NonEditingAuthor: create items; read all; delete own items.
  7. Reviewer: read only.
  8. Contributor: create items only.
  9. AvailabilityOnly: free/busy only. LimitedDetails: free/busy plus subject and location.
  10. None: no access.

Reference for the -AccessRights values used with mailbox folder permission cmdlets.

Shared mailbox full or bouncing

User can't send-as or open a shared mailbox

  2. Grant the specific missing right: Add-MailboxPermission or Add-RecipientPermission.

ProcessData flow — hybrid connectivity: on-prem to Azure
  1. On-prem traffic for Azure ranges goes to the edge firewall or router.
  2. It crosses either an IPsec site-to-site VPN over the internet or a private ExpressRoute circuit.
  3. The Azure gateway in the hub VNet receives it and routes to spoke VNets through peering.
  4. Both sides need matching address ranges with no overlap, plus routes and firewall rules in both directions.
  5. If a tunnel is up but traffic fails, check routes (UDRs), NSGs, and the on-prem firewall rules.

The main paths between a local network and Azure, and what must line up on both sides.

Hybrid network reference architectures — Microsoft Learn ↗ VPN Gateway — Microsoft Learn ↗ ExpressRoute — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessData flow — Azure hub-and-spoke with firewall
  1. Shared services (firewall, gateway, DNS) live in the hub VNet.
  2. Workloads live in spoke VNets that peer to the hub.
  3. User-defined routes send spoke-to-spoke and internet traffic through the firewall.
  4. NSGs add subnet-level allow and deny rules inside each spoke.
  5. Add one spoke per workload or environment so changes stay contained.

The standard Azure network layout. Central inspection and one hybrid link serve many workloads.

Hub-spoke topology — Microsoft Learn ↗ Azure Firewall — Microsoft Learn ↗ Network security groups — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026

ProcessFix a temporary profile ("TEMP" folder)
  1. Run whoami /user while signed in to note the SID; the profile is C:\Users\TEMP.
  2. Create or use a local admin account and sign out the affected user. Reboot to release locks.
  3. Sign in as the admin, then rename the user's folder in C:\Users to add .old (or delete it if no data is needed).
  4. Open regedit and go to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList.
  5. Delete the key for the user's SID (including any ending in .bak).
  6. Have the user sign in to recreate the profile; copy data back from the .old folder.

Back up the old folder first. Deleting the wrong registry key can break other profiles.

A temporary profile appears when Windows cannot load the real one, often after a stale ProfileList registry entry.

whoami — Microsoft Learn ↗ Troubleshoot devices with dsregcmd — Microsoft Learn ↗ Primary Refresh Token overview — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026

net user [username] /delete
rmdir /s /q C:\Users\[username]

Permanent — the user's files are deleted.

Removes the local account and its profile folder. Domain accounts use the profile removal methods above instead.

SafeUser profile location (ProfileList)
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList" /s
# PowerShell: SID -> profile folder
Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList\*" | Select PSChildName,ProfileImagePath
# Path of the current user's profile
echo %USERPROFILE%

Each user SID has a key under ProfileList with a ProfileImagePath value pointing to the profile folder. Keys ending in .bak point to a profile Windows could not load.

ProcessData flow — hybrid identity sync (AD to Entra ID)
  1. Users, groups, and attributes live in on-prem AD; the sync server reads them and writes matching objects to Entra ID.
  2. The sync scheduler runs about every 30 minutes (delta sync). Force one with Import-Module ADSync then Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta.
  3. Sign-in is checked by password hash sync (hash copy), pass-through authentication (agent asks AD), or AD FS (federation).
  4. If a change is missing in the cloud, check the sync server for errors before changing the user.
  5. Only change synced attributes in on-prem AD; cloud edits to synced fields are overwritten.

How identity moves from on-prem Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID, and where to look when a user or password change does not appear.

Entra Connect Sync — Microsoft Learn ↗ Entra Connect sync scheduler — Microsoft Learn ↗ Password hash sync — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
Common issue walkthrough

Device shows not joined / SSO failing

  1. Run dsregcmd /status and check AzureAdJoined, DomainJoined, and AzureAdPrt.
  2. If not joined, re-trigger with dsregcmd /leave then /join, then restart.
  3. Confirm network reachability to login.microsoftonline.com.
  4. Re-check dsregcmd /status for AzureAdPrt: YES after sign-in.

Corrupt profile — "temporary profile" message

  1. Confirm the affected profile object: Get-CimInstance Win32_UserProfile.
  2. Back up user data from the corrupt profile path.
  3. Remove the broken profile object: Remove-CimInstance.
  4. Have the user log back in to generate a fresh profile.

macOS Management (Intune & Apple Business Manager)
ProcessmacOSSet up Apple Business Manager & connect it to Intune
  1. Apply for an Apple Business Manager account at business.apple.com — you'll need a D-U-N-S number and a non-IT contact to vouch for the org. Budget several days for approval (D-U-N-S lookup/verification can take up to 5 business days).
  2. In Intune: Devices > Enrollment > Apple > Enrollment Program Tokens, create an MDM push certificate first, then download the public key (.pem) for the ADE token.
  3. In Apple Business Manager: your name > Preferences > add an MDM Server, upload the .pem, download the resulting MDM Server Token (.p7m).
  4. Back in Intune, upload the token with your Apple ID to finish linking Apple Business Manager to Intune.
  5. Optional: apply for a VPP token (Apps and Books > your tax status) to sync purchased apps/books, and set a default device assignment for new devices.

Start the D-U-N-S/Apple Business Manager application early if you have a deadline — the admin-side verification is the part you can't control or speed up.

Apple Business Manager itself isn't an MDM — it's the portal that lets Apple devices, apps, and organization-owned Apple IDs sync into whatever MDM (here, Intune) you actually manage them with. Only devices added through it are "supervised," which unlocks additional Intune configuration options.

Manage macOS with Intune & Apple Business Manager — IntuneStuff ↗ macOS enrollment — Microsoft Learn ↗ Automated device enrollment for macOS — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessmacOS 13+Add a Mac to Apple Business Manager (Apple Configurator)
  1. Install the Apple Configurator app on an iPhone and sign in with the Apple Business Manager Apple ID.
  2. In network configuration, select your MDM server, then factory-reset the target Mac (Apple silicon or T2 chip, macOS 12.0.1+).
  3. On the Mac's setup screen, hold the iPhone close and scan the "Assign this Mac to your Organization" prompt (or pair manually with the 6-digit code).
  4. In Intune, create an enrollment profile (Devices > Enrollment > Apple > your token > Profiles > Create > macOS).
  5. Sync the token's Devices tab in Intune so the newly added Mac shows up, then assign it to the enrollment profile and save.

If the device is handed to a user before assignment, there's a 30-day provisional window during which they could remove it from supervision/MDM if it isn't yet enrolled with a linked MDM server.

This is the standard way to add a Mac to Apple Business Manager after the fact — useful when a device wasn't purchased through Apple or an authorized reseller (which would normally add it automatically).

Manage macOS with Intune & Apple Business Manager — IntuneStuff ↗ macOS enrollment — Microsoft Learn ↗ Automated device enrollment for macOS — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessmacOS 13+Configure Platform SSO
  1. In Intune: Devices > macOS > Configuration profiles > Create > Settings Catalog > Authentication > Extensible Single Sign On (SSO).
  2. Choose an authentication method: Secure Enclave Key (most secure, hardware-bound, no password sync) or Password (syncs the Entra ID password to the local account — simpler UX).
  3. Set the required keys: Extension Identifier, Team Identifier, Registration Token, Account Display Name, Screen Locked Behavior, and the IdP URLs (login.microsoftonline.com, login.microsoft.com, sts.windows.net — add the sovereign-cloud variants only if needed).
  4. Disable per-user (legacy) MFA for any user going through this setup — it breaks password sync during registration.
  5. Assign the profile to a device or user group, then install the Company Portal app as a macOS LOB app so users can complete registration.

Scope password-setting policies to device groups and compliance policies (with no password settings) to user groups — mixing them onto the same group has been reported to silently break Platform SSO registration.

Platform SSO replaces AD-style directory binding on macOS — it lets the same Entra ID credential unlock the Mac and provide SSO to Entra-backed apps and sites, without a JavaScript-based web login flow.

Configure Platform SSO for macOS — Microsoft Learn ↗ macOS enrollment — Microsoft Learn ↗ Automated device enrollment for macOS — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026
ProcessmacOSEnroll macOS in Microsoft Defender
  1. In Intune: Endpoint security > Microsoft Defender for Endpoint > enable "Allow Microsoft Defender for Endpoint to enforce Endpoint Security Configurations," then confirm the connection is enabled from the Defender portal side too (Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features > Microsoft Intune connection).
  2. Create the required macOS configuration profiles (Settings Catalog or Templates > Custom, using Microsoft's provided .mobileconfig files): System Extensions, Network Filter, Full Disk Access, Background Services, Notifications, Bluetooth Permissions, and Microsoft AutoUpdate.
  3. Create an Endpoint Detection and Response policy and a Microsoft Defender Antivirus policy under Endpoint Security, and assign all profiles to your macOS device/user group.
  4. Deploy the Defender for Endpoint app and the onboarding package (from Microsoft 365 Defender > Settings > Endpoints > Onboarding, OS = macOS, method = Intune) as Intune apps/profiles.
  5. On the device, confirm enrollment through Company Portal, then verify the Defender icon appears and the device shows up under Assets > Devices in the Defender portal.

The kernel/system-extension settings template was deprecated in April 2025 — new deployments should configure System Extensions directly through the Settings Catalog instead.

Each of the six-plus configuration profiles grants one specific macOS privacy permission (System Extensions, Full Disk Access, Background Services, etc.) that Defender's daemon needs — missing any one of them typically shows up as Defender running but reporting incomplete protection.

Intune-based deployment for Defender on macOS — Microsoft Learn ↗ macOS enrollment — Microsoft Learn ↗ Automated device enrollment for macOS — Microsoft Learn ↗ Checked Jul 2026

ProcessData flow — sign-in with Conditional Access and MFA
  1. The app sends the user to Entra ID to sign in.
  2. Entra ID checks the account, then evaluates Conditional Access: user, app, device state, location, and sign-in risk.
  3. If the policy requires it, the user completes MFA or a passkey.
  4. Entra ID issues a token; the app uses it to open the resource.
  5. Check Entra sign-in logs: the Conditional Access tab shows which policy applied and why it passed or failed.

The path every cloud sign-in follows. Most "cannot sign in" tickets are decided at the Conditional Access step.

Common issue walkthrough

Device shows noncompliant / blocked from Conditional Access

  1. Check the device's ComplianceState and identify which specific policy is failing.
  2. Force a sync to push the fix immediately instead of waiting for the next check-in.
  3. Confirm the correct configuration profile is actually assigned to the device.

User stuck at the BitLocker recovery screen

  2. Look up the device's DeviceId, then its recovery key ID.

  4. Read the key to the user, or have them enter it locally if you're remote.

Stuck on "Processing changes"
